p.src:
For any exponent $p$, the binomial series is $\begin{aligned}
(1+\epsilon)^p
&=1+p\epsilon\\
&\quad+\frac{p(p-1)}{2!}\epsilon^2\\
&\quad+\frac{p(p-1)(p-2)}{3!}\epsilon^3
+\cdots .
\end{aligned}$ The exponent may be positive, negative, fractional, or even complex. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the series converges rapidly and each successive term is smaller. We may then stop at whatever order the desired accuracy requires. The zeroth-order term is often the largest, but in the applications below it is frequently a constant and therefore dynamically uninteresting. The first correction is where the motion appears.

p.src:
We normally set $c=1$, so a velocity $v$ means the fraction $v/c$ of light speed. Take $\epsilon=-v^2$. With $p=\tfrac12$, $\sqrt{1-v^2}
=
1-\frac{v^2}{2}-\frac{v^4}{8}-\cdots
\approx
1-\frac{v^2}{2},
\qquad |v|\ll 1.$ With $p=-\tfrac12$, the two minus signs cancel: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}
=
1+\frac{v^2}{2}+\frac{3v^4}{8}+\cdots
\approx
1+\frac{v^2}{2}.$ Many factors of $1/2$ in classical mechanics can be recognized, after the fact, as the first correction in one of these relativistic expansions. The approximation fails as $v$ approaches one; then no finite truncation captures the singular behavior of the exact expression.

p.src: A particle in mechanics need not be elementary. It may be an electron, the Sun, a box of chocolates, or a donut. What matters is that the object holds together well enough for its overall motion to be described by a center of mass. A donut is a useful reminder that the center of mass need not lie in the material itself.

p.src:
In Newtonian mechanics the center-of-mass variables obey $\vec p=m\vec v,
\qquad
K=\frac12mv^2,
\qquad
\vec F=m\vec a.$ These formulas do not care whether the object is elementary or composite. A composite object also contains internal energy. A moving donut, for example, has center-of-mass kinetic energy plus chemical, thermal, and binding energy: $E_{\text{Newtonian}}
=
E_{\text{internal}}+\frac12mv^2.$ The internal term is independent of the overall center-of-mass velocity. Relativity will retain this distinction but will reveal that the internal energy contributes to the invariant mass of the whole object.

p.src: The invariant action was not chosen by guessing a force law. It was chosen as the simplest local Lorentz scalar that reproduces the Newtonian free-particle Lagrangian at low speed. Varying it gives $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x^i}\right)=0,$ so $\frac{dp_i}{dt}=0.$ For fixed nonzero mass this is equivalent to constant four-velocity: $\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau}=0.$ The worldline is therefore a straight line in spacetime. That single geometric statement contains both uniform speed and unchanging spatial direction.
